chapter_text:
CHAPTER 17 - SECANTS, TANGENTS AND THEIR PROPERTIES

Introduction

A circle is the set of all points in a plane that lie at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre). In earlier chapters we studied chords and arcs of a circle. In this chapter we study the different ways a straight line can meet a circle, and the very useful properties that follow. A line in the plane of a circle can do exactly one of three things: it can miss the circle completely (a non-intersecting line), it can cut the circle at two distinct points (a SECANT), or it can touch the circle at exactly one point (a TANGENT). From these simple ideas we build a set of powerful results - the tangent-radius property, the equal-tangents property, the alternate segment theorem, and the product relations for intersecting chords and secants - which are used constantly in geometry problems and proofs.

17.1 SECANTS AND TANGENTS

Imagine a fixed circle and a straight line that we slide steadily toward it. At first the line does not meet the circle at all. As it moves closer it eventually cuts across the circle, meeting it at two points; such a line is called a SECANT. The part of a secant that lies inside the circle, between the two points of intersection, is a CHORD. So every secant contains a chord, and a chord is simply the portion of a secant inside the circle.

If we keep sliding the line, the two intersection points move closer together. At one special position the two points merge into a single point, and the line then touches the circle at just one point without crossing into the interior. Such a line is called a TANGENT to the circle, and the single point where it touches is called the POINT OF CONTACT (or point of tangency). A tangent may be thought of as the limiting position of a secant when its two points of intersection coincide.

Key definitions:
 - Secant: a line that intersects a circle at two distinct points.
 - Tangent: a line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
 - Point of contact: the single point where a tangent meets the circle.
 - A chord is the segment of a secant inside the circle.

Note that from a point INSIDE a circle no tangent can be drawn (every line through an interior point is a secant). From a point ON the circle exactly one tangent can be drawn. From a point OUTSIDE the circle exactly two tangents can be drawn.

17.2 A TANGENT IS PERPENDICULAR TO THE RADIUS AT THE POINT OF CONTACT

The most important property of a tangent is this: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

To picture the proof, let O be the centre of a circle and let a tangent line touch the circle at the point P. Draw the radius OP. Take any other point Q on the tangent line, different from P. Because the tangent touches the circle only at P, every other point of the line lies OUTSIDE the circle. Therefore Q is outside the circle, which means OQ is longer than the radius OP. Thus OP is the SHORTEST distance from the centre O to the tangent line. But the shortest distance from a point to a line is always along the perpendicular. Hence OP is perpendicular to the tangent; that is, the tangent makes an angle of 90° with the radius at P.

A useful consequence (the converse) is also true: a line drawn through a point of a circle, perpendicular to the radius at that point, is a tangent to the circle. So "perpendicular to the radius at its outer end" and "tangent at that point" mean the same thing.

17.3 TANGENTS FROM AN EXTERNAL POINT

From a point outside a circle we can draw exactly two tangents to the circle. Let P be an external point and let the two tangents from P touch the circle (centre O) at the points A and B. The segments PA and PB are called the lengths of the tangents from P.

Theorem (Two tangents from an external point are equal): The lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. In symbols, PA = PB.

Proof outline: Join OA, OB and OP. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, angle OAP = 90° and angle OBP = 90°. In the two right triangles OAP and OBP we have OA = OB (radii of the same circle), OP = OP (common hypotenuse), and the right angles at A and B. By the RHS congruence rule the triangles OAP and OBP are congruent. Therefore the corresponding sides PA and PB are equal, and also the corresponding angles are equal: angle APO = angle BPO and angle AOP = angle BOP.

From this congruence we read off three further facts:
 - The two tangents are equal in length: PA = PB.
 - The two tangents subtend equal angles at the centre: angle AOP = angle BOP, so OP bisects angle AOB at the centre.
 - The line OP joining the centre to the external point bisects the angle between the two tangents: angle APO = angle BPO.

17.4 LENGTH OF A TANGENT

Because the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, we can compute the length of a tangent using the Pythagoras theorem. Let a circle have centre O and radius r, and let P be an external point at distance OP = d from the centre. Let the tangent from P touch the circle at T. Then triangle OTP is right-angled at T (the point of contact), with OT = r as one leg, PT the other leg, and OP = d the hypotenuse.

By Pythagoras: OP^2 = OT^2 + PT^2, that is d^2 = r^2 + PT^2. Solving for the tangent length,

    PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2   and so   PT = sqrt(d^2 - r^2).

This is the LENGTH OF THE TANGENT from an external point.

Worked example: A point P is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. The length of the tangent from P is PT = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(169 - 25) = sqrt(144) = 12 cm.

Worked example: The tangent from a point P is 24 cm long and the radius of the circle is 7 cm. How far is P from the centre? Here OP^2 = PT^2 + r^2 = 24^2 + 7^2 = 576 + 49 = 625, so OP = 25 cm.

17.5 THE ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM

A chord divides a circle into two parts, called segments - the two arcs (with their interiors) lying on either side of the chord. Suppose a tangent touches a circle at a point A, and a chord AB is drawn from the point of contact. The chord makes two angles with the tangent, one on each side. The "alternate segment" for a given tangent-chord angle is the segment lying on the OTHER side of the chord from that angle.

Alternate Segment Theorem: The angle between a tangent to a circle and a chord drawn from the point of contact is equal to the inscribed angle subtended by that chord in the ALTERNATE segment.

In words: if the tangent touches at A and the chord is AB, then the angle between the tangent and the chord AB equals any angle ACB inscribed in the arc on the far side of AB (where C is a point on the alternate arc). The theorem can be proved by drawing the diameter through A and using the tangent-radius property together with the angle-in-a-semicircle result, but for this course the statement and its use in problems are what matter.

Example: If the angle between a tangent at A and a chord AB is 65°, then the inscribed angle in the alternate segment standing on AB is also 65°.

17.6 INTERSECTING CHORDS AND SECANTS (PRODUCT RELATIONS)

When two lines through a circle cross, the products of certain segment lengths are equal. There are three closely related results.

(a) Two chords intersecting inside the circle. If two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at a point P INSIDE the circle, then

    PA . PB = PC . PD.

That is, the product of the two parts of one chord equals the product of the two parts of the other chord. The reason is that triangles PAC and PDB are similar (equal angles from the same arcs and vertically opposite angles at P), so PA/PD = PC/PB, which rearranges to PA . PB = PC . PD.

Worked example: Two chords cut at P inside a circle. One chord is divided into parts 6 cm and 4 cm; the other chord has one part 3 cm. Then PA . PB = 6 x 4 = 24, so if PC = 3 then PD = 24 / 3 = 8 cm.

(b) Two secants from an external point. If two secants are drawn from an external point P, the first cutting the circle at A (near) and B (far), and the second at C (near) and D (far), then

    PA . PB = PC . PD.

Here PA and PC are the near (external) segments and PB, PD the whole secants from P to the far points. Again the result follows from the similarity of triangles PAC and PDB.

(c) Tangent and secant from an external point. If from an external point P a tangent touches the circle at T, and a secant from P cuts the circle at A (near) and B (far), then

    PT^2 = PA . PB.

This is the limiting case of the two-secant result when one secant becomes a tangent (its two intersection points merge at T). It says the square of the tangent length equals the product of the whole secant and its external part.

Worked example: From an external point P, a tangent PT and a secant PAB are drawn. If PT = 6 cm and the near part PA = 4 cm, then PT^2 = PA . PB gives 36 = 4 x PB, so PB = 9 cm, and the chord AB = PB - PA = 9 - 4 = 5 cm.

Worked example: A secant from P meets the circle at A and B with PA = 3 cm and PB = 12 cm. The tangent from the same point P has length PT = sqrt(PA . PB) = sqrt(3 x 12) = sqrt(36) = 6 cm.

SUMMARY

- A line can miss a circle, cut it at two points (a SECANT), or touch it at one point (a TANGENT). The touch point is the point of contact; a chord is the inside part of a secant.
- From an interior point no tangent exists; from a point on the circle exactly one; from an external point exactly two.
- The tangent at any point is PERPENDICULAR to the radius drawn to the point of contact (angle 90°). The converse also holds.
- The two tangents from an external point are EQUAL in length; they subtend equal angles at the centre, and the line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle between them.
- Length of a tangent from an external point at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r is PT = sqrt(d^2 - r^2), since PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2.
- ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM: the angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.
- PRODUCT RELATIONS: intersecting chords give PA . PB = PC . PD; two secants from an external point give PA . PB = PC . PD; a tangent and a secant give PT^2 = PA . PB.

topics.name: Secants and Tangents
topics.description: A line may miss a circle, cut it at two points (secant), or touch it at one point (tangent). Definitions of secant, tangent, point of contact, and the chord as the interior part of a secant; how many tangents can be drawn from interior, boundary and external points.

topics.name: Tangent Perpendicular to Radius
topics.description: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact; the shortest-distance argument for the proof and the converse statement.

topics.name: Tangents from an External Point
topics.description: From an external point exactly two tangents can be drawn; they are equal in length, subtend equal angles at the centre, and the line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle between them (RHS congruence proof).

topics.name: Length of a Tangent
topics.description: Using the tangent-radius right angle and Pythagoras to compute the length of a tangent from an external point: PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2, so PT = sqrt(d^2 - r^2).

topics.name: Alternate Segment Theorem
topics.description: The angle between a tangent to a circle and a chord drawn from the point of contact equals the inscribed angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.

topics.name: Intersecting Chords and Secants (Product Relations)
topics.description: Product relations for lines through a circle: intersecting chords give PA.PB = PC.PD; two secants from an external point give PA.PB = PC.PD; a tangent and a secant give PT^2 = PA.PB.

learning_outcomes.description: Distinguish between a secant and a tangent to a circle and state how many tangents can be drawn from an interior point, a point on the circle and an external point.
State and justify that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, and state its converse.
Prove that the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length and subtend equal angles at the centre.
Apply the equal-tangents property and the angle-bisection property to find unknown lengths and angles in tangent configurations.
Use PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2 (Pythagoras with the tangent-radius right angle) to compute the length of a tangent, the radius, or the distance of the external point from the centre.
State the alternate segment theorem and use it to find angles between a tangent and a chord and inscribed angles in the alternate segment.
Apply the intersecting-chords relation PA.PB = PC.PD and the two-secant relation to find unknown segment lengths.
Apply and justify the tangent-secant relation PT^2 = PA.PB as the limiting case of the two-secant relation, and use it in numerical problems.

chapter_summary.title: Secants, Tangents and Their Properties - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter studies the ways a straight line can meet a circle - missing it, cutting it at two points (a secant), or touching it at one point (a tangent) - and the properties that follow: the tangent-radius right angle, equal tangents from an external point, the tangent length formula, the alternate segment theorem, and the product relations for chords and secants.

sections.heading: Secants, tangents and points of contact
bullets: A secant is a line that intersects a circle at two distinct points; a tangent is a line that touches a circle at exactly one point called the point of contact.
A chord is the part of a secant that lies inside the circle; a tangent is the limiting position of a secant when its two intersection points merge.
From a point inside a circle no tangent can be drawn; from a point on the circle exactly one; from an external point exactly two.

sections.heading: Tangent perpendicular to the radius
bullets: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact (angle 90°).
Proof idea: the radius to the point of contact is the shortest distance from the centre to the tangent line, and the shortest distance is along the perpendicular.
Converse: a line through a point of the circle perpendicular to the radius at that point is a tangent.

sections.heading: Two tangents from an external point
bullets: From an external point exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle.
The two tangents are equal in length (PA = PB), proved by RHS congruence of the two right triangles formed with the radii and the line to the centre.
The line joining the centre to the external point bisects the angle between the tangents, and the tangents subtend equal angles at the centre.

sections.heading: Length of a tangent
bullets: Triangle OTP is right-angled at the point of contact T, with legs OT = r and PT and hypotenuse OP = d.
By Pythagoras, PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2, so the tangent length is PT = sqrt(d^2 - r^2).
Example: a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm has a tangent of length sqrt(169 - 25) = 12 cm.

sections.heading: Alternate segment theorem and product relations
bullets: Alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.
Intersecting chords: if chords AB and CD meet at P inside the circle then PA.PB = PC.PD.
From an external point, two secants give PA.PB = PC.PD, and a tangent with a secant gives PT^2 = PA.PB.

key_takeaways: A line meets a circle in 0, 1 or 2 points: a tangent touches at one point (point of contact), a secant cuts at two (and contains a chord).
The tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and the converse holds.
From an external point the two tangents are equal in length and the centre-to-point line bisects the angle between them.
The length of a tangent from a point at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r is sqrt(d^2 - r^2), because PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2.
Alternate segment theorem: tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.
Product relations: intersecting chords and two secants give PA.PB = PC.PD; a tangent and a secant give PT^2 = PA.PB.

glossary.definition: A line that intersects a circle at two distinct points.
A line that touches a circle at exactly one point without crossing into the interior.
The single point at which a tangent meets the circle; also called the point of tangency.
A line segment joining two points on a circle; the part of a secant that lies inside the circle.
A segment from the centre of a circle to any point on the circle; also its length r.
The distance from an external point to the point of contact of a tangent from it: PT = sqrt(OP^2 - r^2).
A point lying outside a circle, from which exactly two tangents can be drawn to the circle.
The fact that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.
For a chord drawn from a tangent's point of contact, the segment of the circle lying on the opposite side of the chord from the tangent-chord angle.
The angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact equals the inscribed angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.
A region bounded by a chord and one of the two arcs it cuts off.
If two chords meet at a point P inside a circle, then PA.PB = PC.PD, the products of the parts being equal.
For two secants from an external point P, PA.PB = PC.PD, where PA, PC are the near parts and PB, PD the whole secants.
For a tangent PT and a secant PAB from an external point P, PT^2 = PA.PB.
Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side congruence rule for right triangles, used to prove the two tangents from an external point are equal.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Secants, Tangents and Their Properties
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw rough figures where helpful and show your working. Give lengths in the units stated and angles in degrees.

questions.question: Define a secant and a tangent to a circle. State how many tangents can be drawn to a circle from (a) a point inside it, (b) a point on it, and (c) a point outside it.
questions.answer: A SECANT is a line that intersects a circle at two distinct points. A TANGENT is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, the point of contact. (a) From an interior point: 0 tangents (every line through an interior point cuts the circle). (b) From a point on the circle: exactly 1 tangent. (c) From an external point: exactly 2 tangents.
questions.explanation: Basic definitions plus the count of tangents from the three positions.

questions.question: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
questions.answer: Let O be the centre and let the tangent touch the circle at P. Draw radius OP. Take any point Q on the tangent other than P. Since the tangent meets the circle only at P, every other point of the line lies outside the circle, so Q is outside and OQ > OP. Thus OP is the shortest distance from O to the tangent line. The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular. Hence OP is perpendicular to the tangent, i.e. the tangent makes a 90° angle with the radius at P.
questions.explanation: Shortest-distance argument: the radius to the contact point is the shortest segment from centre to the line, hence perpendicular.

questions.question: Prove that the lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
questions.answer: Let P be an external point and let the tangents from P touch the circle (centre O) at A and B. Join OA, OB and OP. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, angle OAP = 90° and angle OBP = 90°. In right triangles OAP and OBP: OA = OB (radii of the same circle), OP = OP (common hypotenuse), and both have a right angle. By the RHS congruence rule, triangle OAP is congruent to triangle OBP. Therefore the corresponding sides are equal: PA = PB. (As a bonus, angle APO = angle BPO, so OP bisects the angle between the tangents, and angle AOP = angle BOP.)
questions.explanation: RHS congruence of the two right triangles OAP and OBP gives PA = PB.

questions.question: A point P is at a distance of 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find the length of the tangent from P to the circle.
questions.answer: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact T, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64. Hence PT = 8 cm.
questions.explanation: Apply PT = sqrt(OP^2 - r^2) = sqrt(100 - 36) = 8 cm.

questions.question: The length of the tangent from a point P to a circle of radius 7 cm is 24 cm. How far is P from the centre of the circle?
questions.answer: In right triangle OTP (right angle at the contact point T), OP is the hypotenuse. OP^2 = PT^2 + r^2 = 24^2 + 7^2 = 576 + 49 = 625. Hence OP = 25 cm.

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at a point P inside the circle. If PA = 6 cm, PB = 4 cm and PC = 3 cm, find PD.
questions.answer: For two chords intersecting inside a circle, PA.PB = PC.PD. So 6 x 4 = 3 x PD, giving 24 = 3 x PD, hence PD = 8 cm.
questions.explanation: Intersecting chords: PA.PB = PC.PD, so PD = 24/3 = 8 cm.

questions.question: From an external point P, a tangent PT and a secant PAB are drawn to a circle. If PT = 6 cm and PA = 4 cm (A is nearer to P), find PB and the chord AB.
questions.answer: The tangent-secant relation gives PT^2 = PA.PB. So 6^2 = 4 x PB, i.e. 36 = 4 x PB, hence PB = 9 cm. The chord AB = PB - PA = 9 - 4 = 5 cm.
questions.explanation: PT^2 = PA.PB gives PB = 36/4 = 9 cm; AB = PB - PA = 5 cm.

questions.question: A secant from an external point P meets a circle at A and B with PA = 3 cm and PB = 12 cm. Find the length of the tangent drawn from P to the circle.
questions.answer: By the tangent-secant relation, PT^2 = PA.PB = 3 x 12 = 36. Hence PT = sqrt(36) = 6 cm.

questions.question: The angle between a tangent to a circle at a point A and a chord AB drawn from A is 58°. Using the alternate segment theorem, find the inscribed angle subtended by AB in the alternate segment.
questions.answer: By the alternate segment theorem, the angle between the tangent and the chord equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment. Therefore the required inscribed angle is 58°.
questions.explanation: Tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment: 58°.

questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 13 cm. A chord of the larger circle is tangent to the smaller circle. Find the length of this chord.
questions.answer: Let O be the common centre. The chord AB of the larger circle (radius 13 cm) touches the smaller circle (radius 5 cm) at a point M. The radius OM to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent chord AB, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so M is the midpoint of AB and AM = MB. In right triangle OMA, OA = 13 (radius of large circle), OM = 5 (radius of small circle). So AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, giving AM = 12 cm. The full chord AB = 2 x AM = 24 cm.
questions.explanation: OM is perpendicular to the tangent chord and bisects it; AM = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = 12, so AB = 24 cm.

questions.question: The tangent at a point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
The tangent at a point is parallel to the radius at the point of contact.
The two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length.
The line joining the centre to an external point bisects the angle between the two tangents from that point.
If a point is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, the tangent length is 12 cm.
The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the inscribed angle in the same segment as the angle.

questions.question: If two chords intersect inside a circle, the product of the parts of one equals the product of the parts of the other.
For a tangent PT and secant PAB from an external point, PT^2 = PA.PB.
A line that cuts a circle at two distinct points is called a ____.
The point where a tangent touches a circle is called the point of ____.
From a point outside a circle, exactly ____ tangents can be drawn.
questions.explanation: Two tangents from an external point.

questions.question: The tangent at any point is ____ to the radius through the point of contact.
The angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact is ____ degrees.
The lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are ____.
The equality of two tangents from an external point is proved using the ____ congruence rule.
If tangents PA and PB are drawn from P and PA = 9 cm, then PB = ____ cm.
The length of a tangent from a point at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r is sqrt(d^2 - ____).
A point 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm has a tangent of length ____ cm.
If a tangent from P is 24 cm and the radius is 7 cm, the distance OP is ____ cm.
By the ____ segment theorem, the tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.
If a tangent-chord angle is 47°, the inscribed angle in the alternate segment is ____ degrees.
If chords meet at P with PA = 6, PB = 4, PC = 3, then PD = ____.
If a secant from P gives PA = 3 and PB = 12, the tangent from P has length ____.
Define a secant and a tangent to a circle.
questions.answer: A SECANT is a line that intersects a circle at two distinct points. A TANGENT is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact, without crossing into the interior.

questions.question: State how many tangents can be drawn to a circle from (a) an interior point, (b) a point on the circle, (c) an external point.
questions.answer: (a) From an interior point: 0 tangents. (b) From a point on the circle: exactly 1 tangent. (c) From an external point: exactly 2 tangents.

questions.question: Explain why a tangent can be thought of as a limiting position of a secant.
questions.answer: A secant cuts a circle at two points. If the secant is moved so that these two points slide toward each other, they eventually merge into a single point. At that position the line touches the circle at just one point and no longer crosses the interior - it has become a tangent. So a tangent is the limiting case of a secant whose two intersection points coincide.
questions.explanation: Two points merge into the point of contact.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a chord and a secant?
questions.answer: A chord is the segment of a secant that lies inside the circle, joining the two points where the secant meets the circle. Every secant contains exactly one chord, and every chord lies on exactly one secant line.
questions.explanation: Chord = interior part of a secant.

questions.question: State the tangent-radius property and give the shortest-distance reason for it.
questions.answer: Property: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact. Reason: every point of the tangent other than the point of contact P lies outside the circle, so its distance from the centre O exceeds the radius OP. Hence OP is the shortest distance from O to the tangent line, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. Therefore OP is perpendicular to the tangent.
questions.explanation: Radius is the shortest segment from centre to line, hence perpendicular.

questions.question: State the converse of the tangent-radius property.
questions.answer: Converse: a line drawn through a point of a circle and perpendicular to the radius at that point is a tangent to the circle. In other words, if a line touches the circle at a point and makes a right angle with the radius there, it is the tangent at that point.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular to radius at its outer end = tangent.

questions.question: A tangent touches a circle of centre O at point T. If P is another point on the tangent, what is angle OTP and why?
questions.answer: Angle OTP = 90°. This is because OT is the radius drawn to the point of contact T, and the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. So the tangent line (which contains TP) makes a right angle with OT at T.

questions.question: Explain why the tangents at the two ends of a diameter are parallel.
questions.answer: Let AB be a diameter with centre O. The tangent at A is perpendicular to the radius OA, and the tangent at B is perpendicular to the radius OB. But OA and OB lie along the same straight line AB (the diameter). Two lines that are both perpendicular to the same straight line are parallel to each other. Hence the tangents at A and B are parallel.
questions.explanation: Both perpendicular to the same diameter, so parallel.

questions.question: Prove that two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
questions.answer: Let tangents from external point P touch the circle (centre O) at A and B. Join OA, OB, OP. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, angle OAP = angle OBP = 90°. In right triangles OAP and OBP: OA = OB (radii), OP = OP (common hypotenuse), right angles at A and B. By RHS congruence, triangle OAP = triangle OBP, so PA = PB.

questions.question: State two further facts (besides PA = PB) that follow from the congruence of triangles OAP and OBP.
questions.answer: (1) The line OP bisects the angle between the two tangents: angle APO = angle BPO. (2) The two tangents subtend equal angles at the centre: angle AOP = angle BOP (so OP bisects angle AOB as well).
questions.explanation: OP bisects both angle APB and angle AOB.

questions.question: Tangents PA and PB are drawn from an external point P. If PA = 3x - 2 and PB = x + 6, find x and the length of each tangent.
questions.answer: Two tangents from an external point are equal, so PA = PB: 3x - 2 = x + 6. Then 2x = 8, so x = 4. Each tangent length = x + 6 = 4 + 6 = 10 (check: 3x - 2 = 12 - 2 = 10). So each tangent is 10 units long.
questions.explanation: Set the tangents equal: x = 4, length 10.

questions.question: Tangents PA and PB from P touch a circle centre O. If angle APB = 80°, find angle AOB.
questions.answer: In quadrilateral OAPB the angles at A and B are right angles (radius perpendicular to tangent), so angle OAP = angle OBP = 90°. The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°. Therefore angle AOB = 360 - 90 - 90 - angle APB = 360 - 180 - 80 = 100°. So angle AOB = 100°.

questions.question: A quadrilateral ABCD has all four sides tangent to a circle. If AB = 8 cm, BC = 9 cm and CD = 5 cm, find DA.
questions.answer: For a quadrilateral whose sides all touch a circle (a tangential quadrilateral), the sums of opposite sides are equal: AB + CD = BC + DA. So 8 + 5 = 9 + DA, giving 13 = 9 + DA, hence DA = 4 cm.
questions.explanation: Tangential quadrilateral: AB + CD = BC + DA.

questions.question: A point P is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the length of the tangent from P.
questions.answer: The tangent PT is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144. Hence PT = 12 cm.

questions.question: The tangent from a point P to a circle of radius 9 cm is 12 cm long. Find the distance of P from the centre.
questions.answer: OP is the hypotenuse of right triangle OTP: OP^2 = PT^2 + r^2 = 12^2 + 9^2 = 144 + 81 = 225. So OP = 15 cm.

questions.question: A point P is 10 cm from the centre of a circle and the tangent from P is 8 cm. Find the radius of the circle.
Two concentric circles have radii 8 cm and 17 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle that is tangent to the smaller circle.
questions.answer: Let O be the common centre and let the chord AB of the larger circle touch the smaller circle at M. Then OM (= 8 cm) is perpendicular to AB at the point of contact and bisects it, so AM = MB. In right triangle OMA, OA = 17 (large radius), OM = 8. AM^2 = 17^2 - 8^2 = 289 - 64 = 225, so AM = 15 cm. The full chord AB = 2 x 15 = 30 cm.

questions.question: From a point 26 cm away from the centre of a circle of radius 10 cm, find the length of the tangent.
State the alternate segment theorem.
questions.answer: The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent to a circle and a chord drawn from the point of contact is equal to the inscribed angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment (the segment lying on the other side of the chord).
questions.explanation: Tangent-chord angle = inscribed angle in the alternate segment.

questions.question: The angle between a tangent at A and a chord AB is 62°. Find the inscribed angle in the alternate segment, and the tangent-chord angle on the other side of AB.
questions.answer: By the alternate segment theorem, the inscribed angle in the alternate segment equals the tangent-chord angle, so it is 62°. The tangent-chord angle on the other side of AB is the supplement along the straight tangent line: 180 - 62 = 118°.
questions.explanation: Alternate segment angle 62°; the other tangent-chord angle 118°.

questions.question: In the alternate segment theorem, from where is the chord drawn, and what is meant by the alternate segment?
questions.answer: The chord is drawn from the point of contact of the tangent. When this chord is drawn, it divides the circle into two segments. For a given tangent-chord angle, the 'alternate segment' is the segment on the OPPOSITE side of the chord from that angle. The inscribed angle in this alternate segment equals the tangent-chord angle.
questions.explanation: Chord from the contact point; alternate = opposite side of the chord.

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at P inside the circle. If PA = 5 cm, PB = 6 cm and PC = 3 cm, find PD.
questions.answer: For intersecting chords, PA.PB = PC.PD. So 5 x 6 = 3 x PD, i.e. 30 = 3 x PD, giving PD = 10 cm.

questions.question: Two secants are drawn from an external point P. The first meets the circle at A and B with PA = 4 cm, PB = 9 cm; the second meets it at C and D with PC = 3 cm. Find PD.
questions.answer: For two secants from an external point, PA.PB = PC.PD. So 4 x 9 = 3 x PD, i.e. 36 = 3 x PD, giving PD = 12 cm.

questions.question: A chord AB and a chord CD intersect at P. Given PA = 8 cm, PB = 3 cm and PC = PD, find PC (the length of half of chord CD through P).
questions.answer: PA.PB = PC.PD. Since PC = PD, this is PA.PB = PC^2. So PC^2 = 8 x 3 = 24, giving PC = sqrt(24) = 2 sqrt(6) cm (approximately 4.9 cm).

questions.question: A secant from an external point P meets a circle at A and B with PA = 4 cm and AB = 5 cm. A second secant meets it at C and D with PC = 3 cm. Find PD.
questions.answer: First find PB: PB = PA + AB = 4 + 5 = 9 cm. Then use PA.PB = PC.PD: 4 x 9 = 3 x PD, so 36 = 3 x PD, giving PD = 12 cm.

questions.question: From an external point P, a tangent PT and a secant PAB are drawn. If PT = 8 cm and PA = 4 cm, find PB.
questions.answer: By the tangent-secant relation, PT^2 = PA.PB. So 8^2 = 4 x PB, i.e. 64 = 4 x PB, giving PB = 16 cm.

questions.question: A secant from an external point P meets a circle at A and B with PA = 2 cm and PB = 8 cm. Find the length of the tangent from P.
questions.answer: By the tangent-secant relation, PT^2 = PA.PB = 2 x 8 = 16. Hence PT = 4 cm.

questions.question: A tangent PT = 12 cm and a secant PAB with near part PA = 8 cm are drawn from P. Find PB and the chord AB.
questions.answer: PT^2 = PA.PB gives 12^2 = 8 x PB, i.e. 144 = 8 x PB, so PB = 18 cm. The chord AB = PB - PA = 18 - 8 = 10 cm.

questions.question: Explain why the tangent-secant relation PT^2 = PA.PB is a special case of the two-secant relation PA.PB = PC.PD.
questions.answer: For two secants from P, PA.PB = PC.PD, where each product uses the near and far intersection points of a secant. If the second secant is rotated until its two intersection points C and D come together at a single point T, that secant becomes a tangent touching at T, and the product PC.PD becomes PT.PT = PT^2. Substituting into PA.PB = PC.PD gives PA.PB = PT^2. So the tangent-secant relation is the limiting case where one secant degenerates into a tangent.
questions.explanation: Let C and D merge into T; PC.PD becomes PT^2.

questions.question: Tangents from an external point P touch a circle of radius 6 cm at A and B. If OP = 10 cm, find the length of each tangent.
questions.answer: Each tangent length PA = PB = sqrt(OP^2 - r^2) = sqrt(10^2 - 6^2) = sqrt(100 - 36) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm. So each tangent is 8 cm long.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A straight line is slid steadily toward a fixed circle. At first it misses the circle; then it cuts across the circle; and at one special position it just touches the circle at a single point.

(i) What is the line called when it cuts the circle at two points?
(ii) What is it called at the special touching position?
(iii) What is the single touching point called?
(iv) How many such touching lines can be drawn from a point outside the circle?
questions.answer:
(i) A SECANT (it meets the circle at two distinct points).
(ii) A TANGENT (it touches the circle at exactly one point).
(iii) The POINT OF CONTACT (also called the point of tangency).
(iv) Exactly 2 tangents can be drawn from an external point.
questions.explanation: Secant, tangent, point of contact, two tangents from outside.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A tangent touches a circle of centre O at a point P. A student draws the radius OP and marks another point Q on the tangent line.

(i) Where does Q lie relative to the circle?
(ii) How does OQ compare with OP?
(iii) What does this tell us about OP as a distance from O to the tangent line?
(iv) What is the angle between OP and the tangent?
questions.answer:
(i) Q lies OUTSIDE the circle, since the tangent meets the circle only at P.
(ii) OQ > OP, because Q is outside the circle while P is on it.
(iii) OP is the SHORTEST distance from O to the tangent line (every other point on the line is farther from O).
(iv) 90° - the tangent is perpendicular to the radius OP, because the shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular.
questions.explanation: Shortest-distance argument for the tangent-radius right angle.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

From an external point P, two tangents are drawn to a circle with centre O, touching it at A and B. The radii OA and OB and the segment OP are joined.

(i) What are the measures of angle OAP and angle OBP?
(ii) Which congruence rule proves triangle OAP congruent to triangle OBP?
(iii) What can you conclude about PA and PB?
(iv) What does OP do to the angle APB?
questions.answer:
(i) angle OAP = angle OBP = 90° (radius perpendicular to tangent at the point of contact).
(ii) The RHS congruence rule (OA = OB radii, OP common hypotenuse, right angles at A and B).
(iii) PA = PB - the two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
(iv) OP BISECTS angle APB (angle APO = angle BPO), and it also bisects angle AOB at the centre.
questions.explanation: Equal tangents by RHS; OP bisects the angle between them.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A point P is 25 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 7 cm. A tangent PT is drawn touching the circle at T.

(i) What kind of triangle is OTP and where is the right angle?
(ii) Write the Pythagoras relation for this triangle.
(iii) Find the length of the tangent PT.
(iv) If instead PT were 15 cm and r were 8 cm, what would OP be?
questions.answer:
(i) Triangle OTP is right-angled, with the right angle at T (the point of contact, where the radius OT meets the tangent).
(ii) OP^2 = OT^2 + PT^2, i.e. OP^2 = r^2 + PT^2.
(iii) PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2 = 25^2 - 7^2 = 625 - 49 = 576, so PT = 24 cm.
(iv) OP^2 = PT^2 + r^2 = 15^2 + 8^2 = 225 + 64 = 289, so OP = 17 cm.
questions.explanation: Right angle at T; PT = 24 cm; OP = 17 cm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A tangent touches a circle at A. A chord AB is drawn from A. The chord makes an angle of 55° with the tangent on one side. C is a point on the arc on the far side of AB.

(i) Which theorem relates the tangent-chord angle to angle ACB?
(ii) What is angle ACB?
(iii) What is the tangent-chord angle on the other side of AB?
(iv) If angle ACB had been 90°, what would the chord AB be?
questions.answer:
(i) The ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM.
(ii) angle ACB = 55° (the inscribed angle in the alternate segment equals the tangent-chord angle).
(iii) The tangent-chord angle on the other side of AB is 180 - 55 = 125°.
(iv) If angle ACB = 90°, the chord AB would be a DIAMETER (angle in a semicircle is 90°).
questions.explanation: Alternate segment theorem: angle ACB = 55°; other side 125°; 90° means diameter.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at a point P inside the circle. It is given that PA = 6 cm, PB = 4 cm and PC = 8 cm.

(i) State the intersecting-chords relation.
(ii) Compute the product PA.PB.
(iii) Find PD.
(iv) Which pair of similar triangles is the basis of this relation?
questions.answer:
(i) For chords intersecting inside a circle, PA.PB = PC.PD.
(ii) PA.PB = 6 x 4 = 24.
(iii) 24 = PC.PD = 8 x PD, so PD = 24/8 = 3 cm.
(iv) Triangles PAC and PDB are similar (equal inscribed angles on the same arcs and vertically opposite angles at P), which gives the proportion leading to the product relation.
questions.explanation: PA.PB = PC.PD; PD = 3 cm; similar triangles PAC and PDB.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

From an external point P, a tangent PT and a secant PAB are drawn to a circle, with A nearer to P than B. It is given that PT = 6 cm and PA = 4 cm.

(i) State the tangent-secant relation.
(ii) Find PB.
(iii) Find the length of the chord AB.
(iv) If a second secant from P had near part PC = 3 cm, find its far part PD.
questions.answer:
(i) The tangent-secant relation: PT^2 = PA.PB.
(ii) PT^2 = PA.PB gives 36 = 4 x PB, so PB = 9 cm.
(iii) AB = PB - PA = 9 - 4 = 5 cm.
(iv) By the two-secant relation PA.PB = PC.PD, so 36 = 3 x PD, giving PD = 12 cm.
questions.explanation: PB = 9 cm; AB = 5 cm; PD = 12 cm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Tangents PA and PB are drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O. It is found that angle APB = 70°.

(i) What are angle OAP and angle OBP?
(ii) Using the quadrilateral OAPB, find angle AOB.
(iii) What does OP do to angle APB?
(iv) State the value of angle APO.
questions.answer:
(i) angle OAP = angle OBP = 90° (radius perpendicular to tangent).
(ii) In quadrilateral OAPB the angle sum is 360°, so angle AOB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 70 = 110°.
(iii) OP bisects angle APB.
(iv) angle APO = 70/2 = 35°.
questions.explanation: Right angles at A and B; angle AOB = 110°; OP bisects angle APB; angle APO = 35°.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two concentric circles share a centre O. The inner circle has radius 6 cm and the outer circle has radius 10 cm. A chord PQ of the outer circle touches the inner circle at the point M.

(i) What is the angle between OM and the chord PQ?
(ii) What special point of PQ is M?
(iii) Find PM.
(iv) Find the length of the chord PQ.
questions.answer:
(i) OM is a radius of the inner circle drawn to its point of contact with the tangent chord PQ, so OM is perpendicular to PQ; the angle is 90°.
(ii) M is the MIDPOINT of PQ (the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it).
(iii) In right triangle OMP, OP = 10 (outer radius), OM = 6. PM^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64, so PM = 8 cm.
(iv) PQ = 2 x PM = 2 x 8 = 16 cm.
questions.explanation: OM perpendicular to PQ; M midpoint; PM = 8 cm; PQ = 16 cm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student claims: 'If a line touches a circle at a point and I draw the radius to that point, the radius and the line always meet at a right angle. And the reverse is also true.'

(i) Is the first part of the claim correct? Name the property.
(ii) State the converse the student refers to.
(iii) Give the reason (in one line) why the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
(iv) At how many points of the tangent is the radius-to-contact-point perpendicular to it?
questions.answer:
(i) Yes. It is the TANGENT-RADIUS PROPERTY: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
(ii) Converse: a line through a point of the circle that is perpendicular to the radius at that point is a tangent to the circle.
(iii) Because the radius to the point of contact is the shortest distance from the centre to the tangent line, and the shortest distance is along the perpendicular.
(iv) At exactly one point - the point of contact.
questions.explanation: Tangent-radius property and its converse; shortest-distance reason.
